catalog.title: Computer Fundamentals
catalog.tagline: How computers work, from the first machines to today
catalog.description: Start here, before any language. Where computers came from, from counting machines and the first electronic computers to the phone in your pocket; why everything inside is binary, and how 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits differ; how text, pictures and sound become numbers, and how a letter gets from a program onto the screen; how logic gates add, how a CPU fetches and runs machine code, and how assembly, the first readable languages and today's languages are built on one another; and what an operating system does. Every lesson has interactive demonstrations and quizzes, and short Python exercises that let you build the ideas yourself.

catalog.title: C
catalog.tagline: The language close to the machine
catalog.description: C is the language of operating systems, embedded chips and the interpreters of other languages: small, fast, and close to the hardware. Starting from the first program, the course covers types, input and output, decisions, loops, functions and arrays, strings, pointers, memory you allocate and free yourself, structures and linked lists, the bugs C lets you make and how to catch them, bit operations, binary data and files, the preprocessor and programs in several files, function pointers, undefined behaviour, how C turns into assembly, a hash table of your own, and finally the advanced language: variadic functions, struct layout and bit fields, modern C from C11 to C23, error-handling patterns, and threads with atomics, then the practice of real C: dynamic strings, generic containers, dates, command-line tools, safe integer arithmetic and random numbers. Every lesson has checked practice compiled with GCC, and every milestone ends with five projects, from small to large.

catalog.title: Assembly
catalog.tagline: x86-64 assembly: talk to the processor directly
catalog.description: Write programs in the processor's own instructions: x86-64 assembly in Intel syntax with NASM, running on Linux. Starting from a program that prints with a system call, the course covers registers, data, Xenon's print and read routines, arithmetic, multiplying and dividing, bit operations and the flags, how numbers become printed digits, compares and jumps, loops, signed and unsigned conditions, if and switch as the compiler writes them, branch-free code, addressing modes, arrays, strings, the stack, buffers and input, call and ret, the System V calling convention, stack frames, recursion, calling and being called from C, reading compiler output, parsing numbers, optimisation, SIMD, ARM64, and finally floating point with SSE, NASM macros, files through system calls, structures, and bit scanning and atomic instructions, then string instructions, division by magic numbers, jump tables, memory from mmap, and arguments and the environment. Every lesson has checked practice, assembled with NASM and run for real, and every milestone ends with five projects, from small to large.

catalog.title: C++
catalog.tagline: From your first program to expert-level modern C++
catalog.description: Thirteen milestones that take you from Hello World to templates, concurrency and performance work. Every lesson has checked practice, and every milestone ends with projects.

catalog.title: Pointers and Memory
catalog.tagline: Addresses, dereferencing, lifetime and allocators, one byte at a time
catalog.description: A whole course on the thing that makes C and C++ hard: memory. What an address is, reading and writing through pointers, pointer arithmetic and strides, reinterpreting bytes, structs and offsets, following chains of pointers, the stack, the heap and object lifetime, ownership, leaks, smart pointers and views, and finally writing your own arena, pool and free-list allocators and seeing how virtual memory and pages work. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course.

catalog.title: Reading Documentation
catalog.tagline: Read any reference page, and turn what it says into code that works the first time
catalog.description: The skill under every other course: finding the right documentation and reading it precisely. How reference pages are laid out, reading C++ signatures, preconditions and undefined behaviour, cppreference and the standard library's return values, complexity and invalidation rules, Microsoft's Win32 pages with SAL annotations, error codes and versioned structures, Python, MDN and Node documentation, man pages, headers and specifications, and finally turning examples into robust code, checking your understanding with small experiments, coping with docs that are wrong, and writing documentation of your own. The practice has you implement functions exactly as documented, including every edge case. It assumes the C++ course up to classes.

catalog.title: C#
catalog.tagline: Modern C# and .NET, from console apps to real applications
catalog.description: Modern C# on .NET, from the first line to a complete, tested application. The course covers types, strings and control flow, methods, collections and LINQ, pattern matching, classes, records, interfaces and inheritance, generics, delegates and events, exceptions and resources, async and await, files and JSON, and how real applications are structured: projects and NuGet, unit tests, dependency injection and desktop UI, and finally the advanced language: operators and indexers, collections in depth, reflection and attributes, Span and performance, regular expressions, and async streams with channels, then LINQ in depth, every kind of pattern, generic math, dates and culture, and variance. Practice compiles and runs on .NET 9 from your browser.

catalog.title: Game Development & Low-Level Programming
catalog.tagline: How games and operating systems really work, from bits to engines
catalog.description: What a computer is really doing when a game runs: bits, memory and addresses, the CPU and assembly, Windows and its processes, debuggers, game engines, modding and the kernel. You read, experiment with live simulations, and build real projects in Visual Studio. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course.

catalog.title: Java
catalog.tagline: Java from the ground up, the way university courses teach it
catalog.description: What a first and second computer-science course in Java cover, in modern Java 25: types, control flow and methods, arrays and ArrayList, recursion, classes, inheritance and interfaces, records, enums and sealed types, generics and the collections framework, exceptions and files, algorithm analysis, searching and sorting, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables and binary search trees built from scratch, lambdas and streams, threads, and finally the advanced language: nested and anonymous classes, the equals and hashCode contract, annotations and reflection, java.time, and binary data, then regular expressions, CompletableFuture and virtual threads, collectors, exact money arithmetic and locales. Practice compiles and runs in your browser.

catalog.title: Python
catalog.tagline: Python for scripting, data and quick ideas
catalog.description: The fastest language to get an idea working in. Starting from the first line, the course covers values, strings and collections, loops and functions, modules and files, classes and errors, the idioms that make Python code short and clear, working with text, CSV, JSON and dates to automate real tasks, and finally the advanced language: decorators, context managers, descriptors, pattern matching, threads and asyncio, and then the practice of real projects: logging, testing with mocks, generic types, binary data, databases and packaging. Every lesson has checked practice that runs real Python 3.13, and every milestone ends with five projects, from small to large.

catalog.title: Working with APIs
catalog.tagline: Call web APIs, connect services together, and reach into C libraries from Python
catalog.description: How programs talk to other programs, in Python: HTTP requests and JSON, reading an API's documentation, API keys, tokens and OAuth with PKCE, signed requests, paging, rate limits, retries with backoff, idempotency and caching, receiving and verifying webhooks, joining two services together with mapping, incremental sync and failure handling, and finally calling C libraries with ctypes. The practice uses small fake servers, so every task runs anywhere and every edge case can be tested; each milestone ends with five projects, from small to large. It assumes the Python course.

catalog.title: Lua
catalog.tagline: The small scripting language inside games and tools
catalog.description: Lua is small, fast and made to live inside other programs: games, game engines, editors, databases and network tools use it for their scripting. Starting from the first line, the course covers values and types, numbers, strings and input, decisions and loops, the table (Lua's one data structure, used as list, dictionary, record and object), functions, closures and recursion, the string library and Lua patterns, metatables, classes and inheritance, modules, errors, iterators, coroutines, files, how Lua is embedded in a C program, and finally sandboxes for untrusted code, weak tables and the garbage collector, and bitwise operators and binary data, then data structures, functional style, serialisation and JSON, object patterns and performance. Every lesson has checked practice that runs real Lua 5.4, and every milestone ends with five projects, from small to large.

catalog.title: JavaScript and TypeScript
catalog.tagline: The language of the web, with types
catalog.description: From the basics of the language to typed, structured programs that run in the browser and on the server. The course covers values and control flow, functions, arrays and objects, classes, errors and modules, asynchronous code with promises and async/await, TypeScript's type system, and the browser: the DOM, events, storage and tooling, a complete web app, and finally the advanced language: regular expressions, Proxy and Symbols, BigInt, dates and Intl, TypeScript’s computed types, and Node.js, then binary data, async generators, cancellation, testing and immutable data. Practice runs in a sandbox in your browser, with TypeScript type-checked as you type.

catalog.title: Rust
catalog.tagline: Memory safety without a garbage collector
catalog.description: Rust from the first program to safe concurrency: Cargo, types and expressions, ownership, borrowing and slices, structs, enums and pattern matching, vectors, strings and hash maps, error handling with Result, modules and tests, generics and traits, lifetimes and trait objects, closures and iterators, smart pointers, threads, channels and shared state, a complete command-line tool, and finally the advanced language: macros, Deref and Cow, unsafe code and FFI, files and processes, and type-state with PhantomData, then error types, operators and conversions, collections, advanced traits and parsers. Best after a first language; the C++ memory milestones make the ownership rules feel familiar. Practice compiles and runs in your browser.

catalog.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
catalog.tagline: The core of a computer-science degree, in C++
catalog.description: Lists, trees, graphs, hashing, sorting and dynamic programming, each built from scratch in C++ and then measured. You learn how to reason about running time, build every classic structure yourself, and choose the right one for a problem, finishing with a spelling checker built on a trie and edit distance. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course: functions, classes, vectors, references and templates.

catalog.title: Game Programming with raylib
catalog.tagline: Make real 2D and 3D games in C++ with a small, friendly library
catalog.description: raylib opens a window, draws shapes, sprites, text and 3D models, plays sounds and reads input, all from a few plain C functions. The course builds a series of small complete games and the game-programming ideas behind them: the game loop, frame time, sprites and animation, collision and platformer physics, cameras, tile maps, enemies and pathfinding, a first 3D scene, shaders, saving and packaging. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course. You build the games in Visual Studio; the practice on the site checks the game logic inside them.

catalog.title: Windows Programming with the Win32 API
catalog.tagline: Native Windows applications, from the message loop up
catalog.description: A full course on the Windows API in C++: handles, errors and Unicode strings, windows and the message loop, painting, input, menus and resources, controls and dialogs, high DPI, Direct2D and DirectWrite, files, the registry, processes and threads, the clipboard and the shell, and packaging, a text editor and a file finder, and then deeper system topics: virtual memory, the console, overlapped I/O and completion ports, services, access tokens and privileges, and COM. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course. You build the programs in Visual Studio; the practice on the site checks the logic inside them.

catalog.title: Networking
catalog.tagline: From packets and sockets to HTTP, packet captures and multiplayer games
catalog.description: How computers talk across networks, and how to write programs that do it: layers and packets, IP addresses and subnets, DNS, TCP and UDP, routing, the socket API, byte order, serving many connections, HTTP by hand, URLs, a tiny web server and what TLS does, capturing and decoding packets from Ethernet up, reliable messaging over UDP with sequence numbers and acknowledgements, and the techniques behind multiplayer games: snapshots, delta compression, interpolation, client-side prediction and lag compensation. It assumes the C++ course.

catalog.title: Processes and Communication
catalog.tagline: Programs that start, watch and talk to each other on Windows
catalog.description: How separate programs on one Windows machine cooperate: what a process is, starting and supervising them, job objects, standard streams, anonymous and named pipes, message framing, serving many clients, overlapped I/O, shared memory with file mappings, ring buffers and seqlocks, named events, mutexes and semaphores, window messages between programs, deadlocks, local sockets, protocol design and serialisation, and securing it all. It ends with single-instance apps, worker processes, out-of-process plugins and a full client and server. It assumes the C++ course and the first milestones of the Win32 API course.

catalog.title: Tool Interfaces with Dear ImGui
catalog.tagline: Fast, practical user interfaces for editors and debug tools
catalog.description: Dear ImGui builds interfaces in a few lines of code inside any game or tool. The course covers setting it up with a graphics back end, every common widget, layout, tables, trees, menus, popups, docking and styling, then the data views tools need, and finishes with a complete level editor and an in-game profiler. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course. You build the interfaces in Visual Studio; the practice on the site checks the logic inside them.

catalog.title: DLLs and Modular Programs
catalog.tagline: Build, export, load and version your own libraries on Windows
catalog.description: Everything about dynamic-link libraries in your own software: exporting functions and classes, import libraries, run-time loading, the loader and its search order, DllMain and its rules, designing stable interfaces across versions, plugin systems and hot reloading during development. It assumes the first milestones of the C++ course. You build the real DLLs in Visual Studio; the practice on the site checks the logic behind each idea.

catalog.title: Reverse Engineering
catalog.tagline: Read compiled programs, find how they work, and build the tools to do it
catalog.description: How to understand a program from its compiled form: the ground rules, the tools, the PE file format, reading x64 disassembly of functions, loops, structs and C++ classes, debuggers from the inside, tracing and finding where data is used, patching and hooking programs you build yourself, and writing your own pattern scanner, memory scanner, disassembler and symbol lookup. It ends with reversing a file format, a protocol and a small virtual machine the course provides. Every target is a program you compiled yourself or one the course gives you. It assumes the C++ course and some x64 assembly (the Assembly course or the Game Development course's milestone 7).

catalog.title: Windows Kernel Driver Development
catalog.tagline: How Windows works underneath, and how drivers are built, tested and debugged safely
catalog.description: An educational course on the Windows kernel and the Windows Driver Kit, done entirely in a virtual machine: kernel architecture, a safe lab with kernel debugging, the I/O model, IOCTLs and a user-mode client, kernel memory, IRQLs and locks, DPCs and work items, observing the system through documented notifications, Driver Verifier, static analysis, secure driver design and signing. The drivers you write only echo, count and log; nothing here touches other programs. It assumes the C++ course and the Win32 API course. You build and run the drivers in a virtual machine; the practice on the site checks the logic inside them.
